trends.trend: US immigration reversal and enforcement build-out
trends.why_it_shapes_daily_life: Decides who is available to build houses, staff care homes, pick crops and fill classrooms: official assumptions cut non-LPR inflows for 2026–2030 by roughly 30–45%, $75bn of detention and ICE money runs to 2029, skilled-visa and refugee channels are nearly closed.

trends.trend: Falling births and near-zero natural population growth
trends.why_it_shapes_daily_life: Fewer babies each year (3.61m in 2025) empties maternity wards, day-care and kindergartens first; deaths are projected to exceed births around 2030, so any local growth depends on migration.

trends.trend: Ageing: the 80+ boom, care demand and pension strain
trends.why_it_shapes_daily_life: About 7.7 million more Americans aged 65+ by 2030 and the 80+ group up roughly 28%: families hunt for care places as occupancy and prices rise, and the retirement trust fund hits its depletion date in 2032.

trends.trend: Enrolment cliff: shrinking school and college cohorts, closures, fewer international students
trends.why_it_shapes_daily_life: The US graduating class peaked in 2025 and shrinks unevenly (Illinois minus 14% by 2030); districts close schools, small colleges merge or close, and foreign students who paid full price are down 15% among new enrolments.

trends.trend: AI rewiring how students learn and what education businesses survive
trends.why_it_shapes_daily_life: Half of teens already use chatbots for schoolwork; homework-help firms are collapsing, computer-science majors are falling 12% a year and PISA scores are at record lows — what school is for, and which credentials pay, is being renegotiated.

sources.update_cadence: every three to four years (2022, 2025, 2029)

ai_passage.text: Students who say they did not use AI to draft text for writing assignments outperformed those who say they did. sources.why_top_or_not: Scores 11 on the rubric, but it covers the same trend as the higher-scoring edtech pick, is a measurement rather than a forecast, and only the press release could be captured (oecd.org blocks downloads).

sources.name: Federal AI-in-schools policy: Executive Order 14277, Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth
sources.publisher: Executive Office of the President (Federal Register)
covers_trends: AI rewiring how students learn and what education businesses survive
sources.what_it_forecasts: Not a forecast: binding directions and deadlines for a White House AI Education Task Force, K-12 AI resources via public-private partnerships, teacher training priorities and a Presidential AI Challenge.
sources.horizon: deadlines of 90–180 days and 12 months from April 2025; no end date

latest_edition.title: Executive Order 14277 of April 23, 2025 (90 FR, published April 28, 2025)

sources.update_cadence: one-off; implementation by agencies; state and district AI policies and College Board/AP changes were not systematically collected

accuracy.why: A signed order with dated obligations on agencies, but it commits process rather than money, can be rescinded by any president, has no adversarial test or error record, and school-level adoption is decided by 13,000 districts it does not bind.

richness.why: Named task force, member agencies, deadlines (90, 120, 180 days; Challenge within 12 months) and programme names; no dollars or school counts.

ai.why: AI is the subject, but the document is from April 2025 and purely qualitative — no quantities to absorb the 2026 acceleration.

ai_passage.text: It is the policy of the United States to promote AI literacy and proficiency among Americans by promoting the appropriate integration of AI into education, providing comprehensive AI training for educators, and fostering early exposure to AI concepts and technology to develop an AI-ready workforce and the next generation of American AI innovators.

sources.why_top_or_not: Sets the direction of official policy on AI in classrooms, but contains no numbers and binds only federal agencies.
